reading.body:
The digital forensics openings here are all federal law enforcement and postal jobs, not AI company roles, posted between late August and mid September 2026.

All three come from USAJobs. The other listed sources, including aggregators, remote boards, and company career boards, contributed nothing to this set. Two are U.S. Postal Service forensic computer analyst positions, in Cleveland, Ohio and Richmond, California, paying $78,160 to $144,820 and $128,740 to $178,390. The third is a Drug Enforcement Administration supervisory chemist for forensic instruction in Quantico, Virginia, at $143,913 to $187,093. The senior and supervisory titles carry the higher bands, which is the only pay pattern three postings can support.

For AI, this is a security function rather than a compute function. Forensic analysts work on devices and data after an incident, so their workload tracks the volume of digital evidence, not the number of accelerators or megawatts. Nothing in these three records speaks to data center construction, power procurement, or grid capacity. None of the three locations is a major AI data center cluster, though three points cannot establish a geographic pattern either way.

What the data does not cover is most of the market. Three postings over roughly three weeks, all federal, all from a single source, say nothing about private sector forensics hiring, remote work, European demand, or any change over time. The count is too small to read as a demand signal.
